newsitem.title: USA: GM transmission workers ratify pact, end strike.
newsitem.headline: GM transmission workers ratify pact, end strike.

text.p: Union workers voted on Sunday to accept a contract at a key General Motors Corp. transmission and wheel plant, ending a four-day strike that threatened to paralyse nearly all North American production by GM.

Officials of United Auto Workers Local 909 in Warren, Michigan, said 89.4 percent of voting members supported the pact, which calls for GM to add about 420 jobs to the plant. About 315 of the workers will be hired within 60 days, while 105 skilled tradesmen will be brought into the plant over the pact's two-year life.
"We think this was a win-win situation for both the company and the union," Peter Belanski, a member of the union's shop committee, said.
As they have with previous settlements, GM officials said the agreement allowed the company to be competitive and also satisfied its employees.
"We believe the agreement provides a framework for meeting the needs of our employees while continuing to allow GM to continue to improve its competitive position," GM spokeswoman Darla Park said.
About 2,800 members of Local 909 walked off the job at midnight last Tuesday after a strike deadline expired without a contract deal. Negotiations continued nearly nonstop during the walkout.

One of the biggest disputes between the two sides was the future of steel wheel production, which GM regarded as a low-tech operation that could be done more cheaply and efficiently by an outside supplier paying less than the $46 an hour that pay and benefits cost GM.

In the deal, according to information distributed to workers, GM agreed to guarantee that wheel production would remain at the plant until 2002. Some wheel work can be moved out of the plant within the next two years, but GM will bring in new work to protect workers' jobs.
GM also agreed to pay workers hired before July 14 about $550 each to settle grievances related to outsourcing. It will pay more than $2 million to settle grievances, the union said.

Park, the GM spokeswoman, said the Warren plant was scheduled to resume production at about 11 p.m. EDT Sunday night (0300 GMT on Monday). It was not immediately clear when the six vehicle assembly lines shut down because of the strike would begin running again.
The Warren plant supplies automatic transmissions for many of GM's front-wheel-drive cars and wheels and suspension control arms for both cars and light trucks.
Parts shortages forced GM to start shutting down plants within a day of the strike. By Friday, it had idled four car plants in Michigan and two at its Oshawa, Ontario, complex.

The shutdowns affected about 16,500 workers, not including the strikers, and led to fears that production disruptions would quickly spread to GM's other North American assembly plants, possibly putting hundreds of thousands out of work.

Two strikes in the second quarter, one at GM's Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, plant for Malibu and Cutlass cars and another at its Pontiac, Michigan, plant for full-size pickup trucks, cost the carmaker $490 million in lost profits.
So far this year, GM has been hit by six strikes. The No. 1 U.S. carmaker has resisted union demands to add jobs as it tries to reduce its workforce through attrition and to pare manufacturing costs.

In Warren the union had demanded that GM add several hundred workers to the plant to offset retirements and ease overtime strains. The union also wanted GM to put a cap on products obtained from outside suppliers.

GM had reportedly offered to transfer torque converter work to the plant to substitute for the wheel work it wanted to move to an outside supplier. But that would have meant loss of torque converter production by UAW workers at GM's Buick City complex in Flint, Michigan. Torque converters are used in auto transmissions.
